explanations.explanation: Moab it is. The man from Bethlehem takes his wife and two sons, and they "went to reside in the land of Moab" (Ruth 1:1). A famine hits, and a whole family packs up and moves countries. That takes guts, friend.
Egypt is a fair guess for a family dealing with a famine. But this text points somewhere else. Ruth 1:1 says they "went to reside in the land of Moab." Egypt doesn't come up in this passage.

Edom sounds like a solid pick, friend, but it's not the one the text gives. Ruth 1:1 says the family "went to reside in the land of Moab." Moab is where Elimelech's family settles, and where the rest of this story starts.

Ruth! Remember that name, friend. Ruth 1:4 says the sons "took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." She walks in quietly here, and she ends up in the middle of the whole story.

Rachel is a real Bible name, but she belongs to a different story. In this one, Ruth 1:4 names the two wives: "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth." Stay with those two names, friend, because they're going to matter.

Dinah is a name from another part of the Bible, so it's easy to see how it popped up. In this passage the sons' wives are "one named Orpah and the other named Ruth" (Ruth 1:4). Ruth is the one to hang on to.

Yes, and this is a heavy one. After about ten years in Moab, "both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband" (Ruth 1:5). I think this one hurts. Naomi has lost everyone she came with.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: No fire shows up in this story, friend. The loss is far heavier than that. Ruth 1:5 says "both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband."

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about Naomi's health or her eyes. What it says is that her sons die. Ruth 1:5 says "both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband." This is a sad moment, so let's treat it with care.

Food! Remember how this whole story started with a famine? Now Naomi hears "that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food" (Ruth 1:6). A cookie stamper knows the sound of good news about a full pantry. That news is what gets her moving toward home.

A king is a big piece of news, friend, but it's not what Naomi hears. Ruth 1:6 says she heard "that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food." Back at the start of the story there was a famine, so food is the news that matters.

Victory would make for a different kind of story. Naomi's news is simpler than that. Ruth 1:6 says "the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food." It's the kind of news you can't wait to bring home.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Right. Naomi tells them, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home" (Ruth 1:8). They're already on the road with her, and she is sending them home. I think she's looking out for them. It's a loving thing to say, even if it's hard to hear.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says anything about the dark or about hurrying, friend. What Naomi says is, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home" (Ruth 1:8). She isn't speeding them up. She's turning them around.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Naomi says. In Ruth 1:8 she tells them, "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home." The two of them have just started the road with her, and she's sending them back.

True! Naomi says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband" (Ruth 1:9). She's praying for good things for both of them. I think this is a mother-in-law with a tender heart.

It's actually true, friend. In Ruth 1:9 Naomi says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." She's asking the LORD to bless each of them with rest and a new home.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: That's it. They answer, "Surely we will return with you to your people" (Ruth 1:10). Naomi sends them home, and they say no. They want to stay with her.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say, friend. They don't offer to wait around. Ruth 1:10 has them say, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They want to go with her, not stay behind.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: A visit sounds nice, but that's not their offer. In Ruth 1:10 they say, "Surely we will return with you to your people." They aren't talking about a visit. They're talking about going all the way with her.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi asks them, "would you wait for them to grow up?" (Ruth 1:13). She keeps laying out the facts. She wants them to see how things really stand before they decide.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't ask that one, friend. She asks about waiting. Ruth 1:13 says, "would you wait for them to grow up?" It's one more reason she gives them to turn around.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: That's not Naomi's question. She isn't sending them on ahead. In Ruth 1:13 she asks, "would you wait for them to grow up?" She's trying to get them to think it all the way through.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi says, "it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). That's how she says it, and I think her heart is heavy. She's carrying a lot, and she says it out loud.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't say that about the people of Judah. She points to something else. Ruth 1:13 says, "it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." These are the words of a woman in deep sorrow.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about the people of Moab turning on her. Naomi gives a different reason in Ruth 1:13: "it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." I think she feels it deeply.
True. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye." She makes her choice, and it's a tearful goodbye. This is Orpah, not Ruth, so keep them straight, friend.
It's true, friend. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye." There were tears first, then a kiss, and then she goes. Ruth is the one who does something different.
Not this time. Ruth doesn't go back with Orpah. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." Orpah goes one way, and Ruth holds on to Naomi.
False is right. Ruth 1:14 says, "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." That little word "but" tells you the two of them part ways. Ruth stays with Naomi.

True. Naomi tells Ruth, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home" (Ruth 1:15). She's still trying to send Ruth home. She's said it before, and she says it again.
It's true, friend. Naomi says, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home" (Ruth 1:15). Naomi hasn't given up yet. She tells Ruth to go after Orpah.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Yes! Ruth says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). Orpah went back to her gods, and Ruth is choosing the LORD. Hang on to that line, friend.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't promise that, friend. Her promise is about people and God. Ruth 1:16 says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God."

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's not part of her promise. Ruth says something bigger. In Ruth 1:16 she says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." She's giving herself to Naomi and to Naomi's God.

Death. Ruth says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me" (Ruth 1:17). She's saying that only death will part them. That's some serious loyalty, friend.
Ruth doesn't say distance. She goes even further than that. Ruth 1:17 says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Only death will do it.
Marriage doesn't come up in Ruth's promise. She names something much bigger. In Ruth 1:17 she says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me."

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ruth 1:18 says, "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her." She has argued with Ruth and sent her home more than once. Now Naomi lets it rest, and they walk on together.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi already tried that, friend, and it didn't work. After Ruth's promise, Ruth 1:18 says, "she stopped trying to persuade her." She doesn't send Ruth back again.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: That's not what happens. Naomi doesn't tell Ruth to wait anywhere. Ruth 1:18 says, "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her."

That's the one. The women of the town exclaim, "Can this be Naomi?" (Ruth 1:19). It's like running into an old coworker you haven't seen in years and trying to figure out if it's really them. They knew her, and they were shocked.
The women don't ask that. What they say is a question about Naomi herself. Ruth 1:19 says they exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?"
They don't call her a stranger, friend. They seem to know her. Ruth 1:19 says the women exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?"

Mara. Naomi says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me" (Ruth 1:20). She wants a new name to match how she feels. It's a sorrowful moment, so let's sit with it a second.
Hannah is a name from another story, friend. Naomi picks a different one. In Ruth 1:20 she says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me."

Leah is a name from another story. Naomi doesn't pick it here. Ruth 1:20 has her say, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." I think she's telling them how deep the hurt goes.

It's the other way around, friend. Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). She left with a husband and two sons, and she's coming back without them. That's why this verse is so heavy.

False is right. Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). She says full on the way out and empty on the way back. I think she's telling them how it feels to come home with so much gone.

Barley! Ruth 1:22 says they "arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest." Remember how this all started with a famine? Now Naomi comes home just as the harvest begins, and that's good news for a cookie stamper's heart.
Wheat is a good guess, friend, but the text says something else. Ruth 1:22 says they "arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest." Barley is the crop coming in.

Olive is a fair guess, but it's not the one. Ruth 1:22 says Naomi and Ruth "arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest." Back in Moab, Naomi had heard the LORD was providing food (Ruth 1:6), and now the barley is coming in.
